chunks: Al-Mudhaffar ibn Ja'far ibn Al-Mudhaffar al-Alawi al-Samarqandi - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Mas'ood al-Ayyashi quoted on the authority of his father, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Nosayr, on the authority of Al-Hasan ibn Musa that his companions quoted on the authority of Ar-Ridha (peace be upon him)

that a man asked him, 'May God settle your affairs! Why did you go to Al-Ma'mun?' He was somehow blaming the Imam for this. So Abu Al-Hasan Ar-Ridha (peace be upon him) asked him, 'Hey you! Which is nobler, a Prophet or a Trustee?' He said, 'Certainly a Prophet.' He asked, 'Which is nobler, a Muslim or an atheist?' He replied, 'Certainly a Muslim.'

He said, 'Indeed al-Aziz - the king of Egypt - was an atheist while Joseph (peace be upon him) was a Prophet. And Al-Ma'mun is a Muslim and I am a Trustee. Joseph (peace be upon him) asked al-Aziz to establish him as a leader when he said, "Set me over the store-houses of the land: I will indeed guard them, as one that knows." But I was forced to do so.'
Set me over the store-houses of the land: I will indeed guard them, as one that knows.

And he (peace be upon him) said regarding His words, 'Set me over the store-houses of the land: I will indeed guard them, as one that knows,' he said, 'Guarding what is in my hands, knowing every language.'

key_terms.الْعَزِيزُ: Al-Aziz, the chief official/king of Egypt in the time of Joseph
key_terms.الْوَصِيُّ: The Trustee, a title for the Imams denoting their role as successors to the Prophet

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali ibn Musa Ar-Ridha accept Al-Ma'mun's appointment as heir apparent?
ai.summary: Imam Ar-Ridha (a.s.) employs a dialectical analogy, comparing the hierarchy of Prophet vs. Trustee to Muslim vs. Polytheist, to demonstrate that his status as a *Wasi* (Trustee) is superior to Caliph Al-Ma'mun's status as a mere Muslim. He clarifies that Joseph’s request for governance was not an assertion of inherent superiority but a pragmatic necessity to preserve the faith, whereas the Imam’s acceptance of the Caliphate was a divinely compelled duty to safeguard the community from corruption. This narrative underscores the Shia doctrine of *Ikrah* (compulsion) in the Imams' political engagements, distinguishing their spiritual authority from the temporal power of the Umayyads and Abbasids.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 40-1 Al-Mudhaffar ibn Ja’far ibn Al-Mudhaffar al-Alawi al-Samarqandi - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ja’far ibn Muhammad ibn Mas’ood al-Ayyashi quoted on the authority of his father, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Nosayr, on the authority of Al-Hassan ibn Musa (al-Khashshab) that his companions quoted on the authority of Ar-Ridha’ (a.s.) that a man asked him, “May God settle your affairs!

Why did you accept this affair and go to Al-Ma’mun? He was somehow blaming the Imam (a.s.) for this. However, Abul Hassan Ar-Ridha’ (a.s.) asked him, “Hey you! Please tell me whether a Prophet is nobler or a Trustee?” The man said, “Certainly a Prophet.” He (a.s.) asked, “Is a Muslim nobler or an atheist?” He replied, “Certainly a Muslim.”

He (a.s.) said, “Indeed al-Aziz - the king of Egypt - was an atheist while Joseph (a.s.) was a Prophet. And Al-Ma’mun is a Muslim and I am a Trustee. Joseph (a.s.) asked al-Aziz to establish him as a leader when he asked the king of Egypt, “Set me over the store-houses of the land: I will indeed guard them, as one that knows (their importance)” But I was forced to do so.

And when he (a.s.) said God’s words, ‘Set me over the store-houses of the land: I will indeed guard them, as one that knows (their importance).’ He said that since he knew well how to take care of it and knew all the languages.
